utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the Chamber regretted very much that last Thursday, that we have you made waiting for quite a while and then we couldn't hear any further testimony of yours. Therefore, apologies for that, but the situation was such that we couldn't do otherwise. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination-in-chief, and I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at Dr. Tabeau's report as to Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can call up P7449, and it will be page 45 in the English and page 58 in the Serbian, and it will be the second-to-last paragraph in English, and it will be the paragraph just before the main findings of Dr. Tabeau in both languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I get the report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we still have everything in the hands of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a hard copy of the report available for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so on the Serbian version that's on the screen, it will be the paragraph right in the middle of the page, and it will be towards the bottom of the page in the English. And the paragraph starts off by saying: "The matching methodology and sources used for this report were the same as those applied in the compilation of all OTP lists of the 1995 Srebrenica victims, starting with the list of 2.000" --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't find this. Is it in the Serbian version on page 58?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On page 58, it is the middle of the screen and the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So to begin again: "The matching methodology and sources used for this report were the same as those applied in the compilation of all OTP lists of the 1995 Srebrenica victims, starting with the list of 2.000 tendered into evidence in the Krstic case and the latest one being the 2013 Srebrenica update tendered in the Mladic case in November 2013." Now, professor, I know that you are familiar with the list of -- of -- of criteria from the Srebrenica report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can call it up so that we can all be refreshed of that. It's Exhibit P01900, and it will be a -- starting on page 81 in the English and page 86 in the Serbian of that report. And in both versions the list continues on to the following page, but if we can have just the first aspect of that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, now we have on the screen the criteria from the Srebrenica report that Dr. Tabeau has just referenced in her Tomasica report. What conclusions can we draw based upon what Dr. Tabeau has told us in her Tomasica report about the matching methodology she employed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by what is written here, the matching was done in accordance with 72 criteria, just as with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in your opinion, how reliable are results obtained from such a method of matching using these 72 criteria?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With 72 criteria, you can match anything you like. But degree of reliability can be seen from the criteria where, according to the first criteria, which shows high degree of likelihood that these are one and the same individuals in two sources, and matching, if I'm not mistaken, it's only 16 per cent. I think this is a mistake. It says 33.251 but it is rather 3.251, because the ICRC database includes around 20.000 first and last names, and they are matching with it. I'm not exactly certain but I think it's 3.251 as compared to 20-odd thousand, so around 16 per cent, judging by the first criterion as I say, it's a high degree of likelihood that it's one and the same person. So it could be said with a great degree of likelihood that they really have been matched. There is another error in the first criterion which is to be found in English. If I remember probably in English it says, inter alia, that it's compared with the place of death. In the Serbian version, this does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't matter. Because comparisons are made with the census, as they say. The population census does not include the location of death. Only the living are included in it. So I think it's just a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think we may have dealt with that the last time you were here. Now, in relation to the matching criteria or keys in the Tomasica case, I asked Dr. Tabeau about the same, and I'd like to go through her answers before the Trial Chamber with you to see if we can better understand them. First, at transcript page 36.790, lines 5 through 20, we have the following testimony which I will read to you: "Q. Okay. Now if we can turn to your report, which I believe is P7449, relating to Tomasica, and if we could turn to the -- for now, page 1 in both languages, and this is the contents of your report. Doctor, last time you were here, we talked about over 70 criteria or you called them, I think, keys, which you used when matching names with the various databases. This report on Tomasica that is before us does not seem to identify how many keys were used in the Tomasica report, does it? "A. It is not so that I provide with every report an overview of matching criteria I have used for matching various lists with each other, so this particular report does not contain such a list. The list you have mentioned was made available as part of the 2009 integrated Srebrenica report provided as example, an explanation of how the matching is done. I will stand by this list and the criteria, but in every project, I use some of these criteria as they are in this table and some additional criteria formulated in line with the logic of that table." What comment do you have as to Dr. Tabeau saying that she uses some of the criteria on the Srebrenica table and formulates additional ones in line with the logic of that table for every project that she does?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what would be professionally correct would be for her to say which criteria of the 72 she used, and what additional criteria mean, it would also be professionally correct to explain that. That was why I requested to receive the matching criteria. I know what they were for Srebrenica, though I don't know which ones she used. And as for additional criteria, it's not only Dr. Tabeau who can know. We have to know too in order to be able to assess whether they are sufficient for matching, what they imply, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By the way, were you able to find the matching criteria on your own that Dr. Tabeau used anywhere in the demography unit materials that were made available to you when you visited the Tribunal in January of this year?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither in the materials when I was here, nor in any of the reports that I have read. And I've read quite a few reports by Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I asked Dr. Tabeau another question when she was here testifying about her Tomasica report, and I'd like to read to you the testimony at transcript page 36.790, line 21, through 36.791, line 3, and it goes as follows: "Q. That's entirely what I expected, doctor, and that's why I asked you to precisely tell us how many matching criteria or keys were used for the Tomasica report and what precisely those keys were. "A. You would have to be more specific about your question. If you say matching of the Tomasica list, then have you to tell me with what source, and then I can explain more specifically what was the criteria based about. Still, I will not give you the concrete criteria because I don't have them at hand." Professor, what do you make of Dr. Tabeau's answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that Dr. Tabeau is playing with you. She is telling you to be more specific and tell her what source you have in mind. You're a lawyer, and as she thinks that the Trial Chamber is not expert in methodology, she probably thinks also that are you not. Regardless of which source you had in mind, there must be a criterion which she had to state and then say, I compared it with such and such criteria. What is especially interesting here is that she says you should mention the sources. It means that for each separate source, she used separate criteria. So, for example, for the ICRC source and the population census, one set of criteria; then for ICRC and the book from Prijedor, another set of criteria; for third sources, for example when comparing some sources, a third set of criteria, and so on. So what is professionally correct and what is required is to state the criteria you have been using. It's symptomatic that she is not using one and the same key for all sources or one and the same set of keys. Why she is not doing that, well, that is something she would have to explain, why she changes the criteria from one source to another. And not in some order, but keys in general, as criteria, somewhere she uses all the information, somewhere only the first and last names, and so on. So it would have been proper if Dr. Tabeau had told you, or if she had written that, inserted a footnote and said, I used this and this for such and such a source, and so on. And asking you to state which source you have in mind, I think that's just playing with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By the way, professor, in your opinion, how difficult would it be for a demography expert who has conducted matching according to keys or criteria to provide those keys or criteria to someone else to review the results?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that shouldn't be difficult at all. It's a methodological procedure that you apply. How difficult it was to obtain all the criteria that we have in front of us now that were used for Srebrenica, the doctor did not write those criteria later on, or anyone else. When you start with matching, you have to set the criteria and that mustn't be difficult. When you begin this work, you have to know exactly what criteria you are using to compare units from two different sources. So somebody has to write it down. You cannot do it off the top of your head, because if you do, you simply don't know what you have done or not. So I do not consider that difficult at all. It's just a question of good will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can present to you what Dr. Tabeau testified about at our trial on this topic, that's at transcript page 36.791, lines 4 through 7. And again, I would read that portion of the transcript and then ask you some questions. And it goes as follows: "Q. Do the concrete criteria exist somewhere in your office? "A. If you mean in a form of the list, like the list of 70, then my answer is no, they don't. Other than that, I can provide you with the logic of my matching for any two sources that you will mentioned." Professor, from the standpoint of professional, scientific practice of demography, what is your comment as to Dr. Tabeau's assertion that the matching criteria she used do not exist in the form of a list but that she can provide us with the logic of the matching?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I find it very strange. Let me repeat: When you start a matching process, you set the criterion. And if you don't write it down, for me it's unbelievable. The logic of matching cannot be explained unless you have the criteria. You cannot match anything logically if you do not know what you're matching it by, on the basis of what. You have to know the element on the basis of which you're matching something. So you can deduce the logic and say, I'll take the name, the first name, last name, a date, but the logic itself doesn't mean anything unless you have a key that you're applying. So, to be honest, I do not understand what the logic of matching means without criteria. Once you set a criterion and when you see if it's adequate, if it's logical and if it makes any sense to do the matching based on it or not. So I don't really understand, and I have never heard, that a logic of matching is provided. I know that criteria for the matching are provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to continue with additional items that Dr. Tabeau testified about at transcript 36.793, lines 3 through 19, and they read as follows: "But I think that Mr. Ivetic sees the process of matching in a very formal way, in the sense that one starts from a formal list of criteria and then goes through the entire list to end with a result at the end. As a matter of fact, a very long list of criteria, say 70, might be finished after five first steps because the records simply match very well, and then there is no need even to go through the rest of the list. So the matching process is basically cross-referencing of two related lists, or two lists expected to be related to each other, and mainly by comparison of the names on the two lists and dates of birth, other information on the lists, one draws conclusions about the similarity of potentially related cases. If there is an identity of reporting on the two lists of a given person, then a match can be easily declared. If there are slight differences in the spelling of names or in the dates of birth, then one has to decide whether the differences are acceptable and a match can be declared or a match cannot be declared." Professor, what can you tell us about what we have just heard from the testimony of Dr. Ewa Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctor notes that you are seeing the matching process formally, but it is a formal procedure. It's not an informal procedure of any kind. She then says that she cannot set 72 or 100 criteria and then start and see that they're fine after five. The problem is that when you start with the first criterion you have to decide what's a high degree of likelihood. So if that one works, you don't go any further. But if that one does not work, then you have to reduce the criterion, make it shorter. The shorter a key is, the likelihood of matching is higher. But the likelihood of good data is smaller. If you say that units from two sources are to be compared by the first and last name, the name of the father, the place and date of birth, and you find identical information, then the likelihood that it is one and the same person is very high indeed. But if you did not receive that, then you might say, Well, I am not going to use all the criteria. I have to shorten it. Let me look by using first and last name, father's name, and the year of birth, without the place of birth, and I'll get matching again. But if I'm not happy with it again, I can shorten it again and I can say, Well, just the initial of the first and last name, the full father's name, and the year of birth. And then on the basis of that, I will once again get a certain number of matches with all similar initials, but, for example, you can use the year range of three rather than five; from 1949 to 1952, for example. And then you review all the information, then the doctor or whoever is doing it may say, Well, this is the one. So it's not identical by similar. On the first or second day when I testified we had a chance to see table 1, where in most cases the first name is the same, the father's name is the same, and the last name is the same, but the places of birth and the dates of birth are completely different. The doctor judged that this was one and the same person who has been matched. But how, by applying what kind of logic, that's something I really cannot go into. Making such decisions is something that has to be stated. For the first criteria I guarantee such and such a number. For the fifth, such and such. I have made such decisions to do such and such a thing and that applies to such and such a percentage of the total material that you are matching. I also don't know what Dr. Tabeau understands by small differences. Is a different place of birth or a different date of birth considered a small difference? I think that Dr. Tabeau should have provided explanations for all of these, and professionally it could have been done. We have the criteria in front of us. We could have assessed the degree of matching. She could have said, Because, here, there's around 16 per cent of matching. According to another criterion, it could be 20 per cent. According to another, 20 or 60 per cent. So that's the basis on which you decide about the degree of combining the data from two sources. I think that Dr. Tabeau is intentionally concealing the calculations so that the degree of combinations is difficult to assess. But if you look at the 72 criteria and see that it's matching from ICRC 20-odd thousand people as compared to 4 million people, on the basis of this you can assess the degree of combinations. The exact number, what is matched with what, and you can see what the degree of combination is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at your report, which is 1D06189 and has been marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue -- Could you tell us why you think that Dr. Tabeau is intentionally concealing the calculations? Do you have any reason to believe that she intentionally wants to deceive this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if she promised the lawyer to provide the criteria and didn't, and then if I requested in writing that she provide the criteria, she still didn't, then I think that she is intentionally concealing them. If the additional criteria are not stated anywhere, I could have taken these 72, no problem, but the doctor claims there are additional criteria for various sources of information, she doesn't even explain one -- why she didn't provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, you say "if she promised the lawyer to provide the criteria." Did she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, during the examination a few days ago, we heard that she had promised and didn't. The lawyer quoted that, but he hasn't received the criteria. Later, I requested them in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To Dr. Tabeau directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw Dr. Tabeau twice in my life ten years ago. I address my requests to the Defence team, and I suppose they forward these requests to Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt for one second. We have now a list on the screen. I think it shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then we also have the wrong document, then, it would appear. I'm looking for what has been marked for identification as D1464, which should correlate to 1D6189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you asked for. Just to continue, Mr. Ivetic, was there a direct or not a direct request to Dr. Tabeau to -- in writing, because we would like to know then. And also we would like to know why, if there was no response that, why the Defence -- at least I do not remember whether you asked us to support any request for further information by Dr. Tabeau. Because -- could you provide us with some additional information on when and how and in what wording requests were sent to Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I can try to assist. We looked at the transcript of Dr. Tabeau's testimony here in relation to Tomasica from last year where I asked for those matching criteria to be provided, and Dr. Tabeau indicated it would take some time and she couldn't recreate them in the courtroom now. And then after that, I believe it was in October of last year, it was the day before I went to Serbia and the day before Dr. Dunjic's death, that I believe the written list was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor in a meeting between Mr. Tieger and Mr. Lukic. That written list was the request of Professor Radovanovic. And I know that the Prosecution had that list because in subsequent meetings with Ms. D'Ascoli and Mr. Traldi, I met with them and they had that list translated into English. And on that list I believe -- I don't have it front of me, but I think it was -- request number 12 or 13 was for the matching criteria that Dr. Tabeau had used in her Tomasica report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there are, well, relatively strong accusations against Tabeau as intentionally concealing something. Is there any way that the parties could agree to provide to the Chamber, because we will take that seriously, first of all, the exchange of written reports, because Ms. Radovanovic says, Well, we requested it in writing and now it -- I do understand that there has been a communication between the parties including lists -- well, a list in itself is not yet a request. The Chamber also notes that if there was no follow-up, that as far as I remember, but please correct me when my recollection doesn't serve me well, that never we were asked to support or give further orders to the Prosecution to present certain evidence such as these kind of matching criteria used in relation to Tomasica. So it's all pretty tough, but I'd like to know, and perhaps my colleagues as well, what exactly is at the basis of that. Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I might be able to provide a shortcut to this exchange. We received the list of 13 requests that Dr. Radovanovic wished to have access to when she came here on the 5th of November, 2015. Number 13 on that list was "list of criteria used as basis for matching and linking from different information sources." And following our consultations, we presented the list from P1900, the list of 72 criteria which includes all of the primary criteria that Ewa Tabeau used for this report other than any individual decision-making on particular records. We put that in the folder that Dr. Radovanovic had access to when she came here in January, and we received no further communications indicating that that was unacceptable or that they were looking for some other type of information, and that's where it was left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that where Dr. Tabeau testified that she didn't have a -- she couldn't reproduce immediately what criteria she used, that she would have make that, and at that time I think there 70 criteria list -- was -- was in existence. So later on it's a matter of access to something Dr. Tabeau may have testified, if it's the same, that it did not yet exist and still had to be produced. And there is a chance there is some mal-communication and at least there was no follow-up with the Chamber. And if I understand you well, Mr. File, also not once you had provided what you have provided, that there was no additional request as to: This is not what I meant, I want something else, which then, of course, also never reached the Chamber. That's -- Mr. Ivetic, is there any -- do you agree that the details given by Mr. File are about the same you talked about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Except for the date of November 5th, I'm not sure of that date, but it was either late October, early November, when that was provided. And then I also then quote the testimony of Dr. Tabeau at transcript page 36.790, where she indicated for Tomasica she started with the 2009 integrated Srebrenica report and then used additional criteria formulated in line with the logic of that table. So we don't have that additional criteria that Dr. Tabeau mentioned when she testified as to the Tomasica report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm at this moment primarily interested in where it went wrong to the extent that Dr. Radovanovic is now saying that Ms. Tabeau intentionally tried to conceal, where it may have gone wrong in terms of communication, what -- who is asking what from whom, and was the Chamber ever invited to assist in resolving such problems. That's -- was what I was mainly focusing at this moment. I intervened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you intervened. I think it was your question, actually, and then you posed a question to me. So I don't know if Your Honours have finished with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I intervened. Ms. Radovanovic has answered my request that she did not make any written request herself directly to Dr. Tabeau, and we now better understand what kind of a request it was and what response was received on that. And it was all about my question what makes you believe that there was an intention to -- to conceal. That's where I intervened. And please resume from where I intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We now have Professor Radovanovic's report as to Tomasica on the screen. I'd like to have page 17 in English and page 22 in the original Serbian, and it will be paragraph number 47 that I'd like to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, professor, we have your paragraph 47 on the screen. I'd like to focus on the second half of that paragraph, and it starts in middle of that paragraph, where you say: "Reassociation means that another body part of an already identified person was subsequently found and should be joined to the initial already identified findings. Therefore, no new identifications are in question but the reassociation of found skeletal parts of an already identified person whose whole body has not been exhumed. The Prosecution expert witness knows that for she notes that: The reassociations cases of positive identification of body parts additional to the already existing positive match reports for the main cases. The reassociations are not counted as additional cases of positive identification, they express the fact that the [sic] bodies were sometimes dismembered within one grave or fragmented between more graves. Why then does the expert add up the [sic] parts of the same whole, although it is clear to her that all the reassociated cases are parts of some main cases?" Professor, you pose a question here. I would ask it of you and see what answer you would come up with.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table is presented in an incorrect way, and I believe it is pure manipulation. If these are reassociated cases, then it involves parts of the bones of some people that the doctor refers to here as main cases. So it's the same people and parts of their bones. In the course of identification, it happens that one doesn't find the whole body, that later some body parts are found subsequently and added to the body. You can't add it up and say that you have a total of 712. 712 what? A reassociated case is, in fact, the main case. Part of the main case. The doctor says there are 378 cases out of which 334 bones belong to them. So you can't add it up. And what does it mean, a total of 712? Is it 712 bones? No. Is it 712 identified people? No. So this table has the purpose of creating confusion, in my deep conviction, because this is not the way to present something and to add it up. Dr. Tabeau, within the tables that she attaches to the report, and that is on -- about 100 pages, she numbers them from 1 to 712, so you can't take a single table and follow the normal numbering from 1 to N. If Dr. Tabeau knows exactly how many people have been identified, although I don't agree with it, then you take it 1 to X. First of all, I believe this is not the way it should be done. Second, I believe the purpose is to create confusion. Because Dr. Tabeau understands perfectly well the statistical methodology, and she is counting on others not being familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to Dr. Tabeau's report, which is P7449, and if we take a look at Table 18, which is to be found on page 32 in the Serbian at the bottom of that page, and in English it will be the middle of page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now that we have Table 18 up in both languages, can you please explain to us what you want to say about this table of Dr. Tabeau's.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a piece of demographical data and I call it statistical exhibitionism. The number of shots fired at somebody has nothing to do with demography. Demography doesn't deal with any number of shots. It deals with the cause of death by external effects, such as gun-fire, poisoning, et cetera. So since Dr. Tabeau has not a single demographic indicator shown normally in demography within statistical reports, she uses the number of gun-shots. The number of gun-shots has nothing to do with demography. Demography deals with cause of death by gun-fire. I suppose -- in fact, I don't suppose, I know she takes this from Dr. Clark. You have an absurdity here. She calculates how many shots were sustained by each victim on average, and she gives you a conclusion, saying that the whole group took 740 shots, up to 750. This has nothing to do with science.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a look at P7453 in e-court, and this will be the PowerPoint presentation that Dr. Tabeau used in court the last time she was here, and if we could have page 9, which is slide 9, in both languages up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While that is coming up, I would like to put a question to the witness. Ms. Radovanovic, you said: "Demography deals with cause of death by gun-fire." Why are you then saying that the number of gun-shots has nothing to do with demography? The number of gun-shots may also indicate something about the cause of death. I really don't understand why you made this distinction. Could you explain it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't think we understood each other well. Demography deals with the cause of death. Cause of death, for instance, may be gun-shot wound to the head. And the demographer is not interested whether death was caused by 1 or 75 shots. He is looking at the cause of death, and he looks at relevant information. He knows that the cause of death is an external impact. And he doesn't see it even in the relevant sources. Here, Dr. Tabeau saw in Dr. Clark's report the number of gun-shots, and since she has no relevant demographic indicator and she is not able to say the cause of death is violent, caused by this or this, death by poisoning, death by gun-fire, from fire-arms, et cetera, instead she cites the number of shots. This has nothing to do with demography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at slide that we have on our screen, and during trial at the intervention of the Trial Chamber, Dr. Tabeau corrected the table we see in front of us. And that was at transcript pages 36.734 to 36.733. And the correction of Dr. Tabeau says we have to delete the 13.2 per cent listed under "unavailable" on Table 5, and the Serb translation on the left has taken into account this correction of Dr. Tabeau, but in English we still see 13.2 per cent under "unavailable." In your opinion, is the correction by Dr. Tabeau of deleting the 13.2 per cent unavailable leading to an accurate demographic representation of this data?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think one of the Judges asked whether these 13-plus per cent should be deleted because the total exceeded 100 per cent. The doctor said yes. And this is an error. You can't delete something that exists. These 13-plus per cent exist. But if you see that the total exceeds 100 per cent, then it means you made an error in calculation, and you have to recalculate the percentages. The error here lies in the fact that Dr. Tabeau counts the unavailable as Muslims, and she say there are 95 per cent of Muslims, which is not correct. If there are 330, if I see well, it's not 95 per cent of the total. It's about 80-something per cent. And you can see that very well in this next part where she talks about Prijedor and the ARK. Look at the unavailable, 522. The field is blank. And these 522 is about 20 per cent of the total. And, again, Dr. Tabeau ascribes it all to Muslims. How does she know that these unavailable are Muslim by ethnicity? Muslims are 80-plus per cent if these 522 are about 20 per cent of the total. So this is not about deleting an element that exists. The point is in the calculation. And this calculation is done on the premise that all of them are Muslims. I wouldn't mind if Dr. Tabeau put in a footnote saying: I believe that these unavailable are Muslims for these and these reasons. Because we are talking here about matching, and the only ethnicity -- the only source of seeing ethnicity is the census. If she found 522 or 44 unavailable by ethnicity because she couldn't identify them according to 72 criteria, then it would be fair to leave it at that and to change the share of other ethnicities. That is to say, the Muslims. If Dr. Tabeau knows some other source that tells her that these people are Muslims, then she should have put in a footnote saying: I believe the unavailable are, in fact, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, you said "if there are 330, if I see well," perhaps it's an interpretation or a typing issue. The table says 320, just for the record, and not 330. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Judge Fluegge. My eyesight is not too good. I can see now. It's been enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are at the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Ivetic, and thank you for reminding me. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We very briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness, Your Honours, I can perhaps put on the record that the Defence does not consider the tendering of the 72 criteria from the Srebrenica report to be the final answer as to the matching done for Tomasica or even for Srebrenica because while the criteria are there, we don't have the matching results which would allow us to know under what criteria or what number of items matched. We don't have that for the Tomasica report, nor do we have that for even the Srebrenica list because, of course, the 72 matching criteria and the results in that part of the Srebrenica report relate to the ICRC list and the census, not the list of victims for Srebrenica, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. I believe that what Mr. Ivetic is referring to now is a matching log, and that is different from the matching keys or criteria that we've been discussing, and I just wanted to put that on the record as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now everything is on the record. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to return to your report, which is now D1464 marked for identification, and I would like to look at page 22 in the English and it will be page 29 in the Serbian, and it will be paragraph number 66.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to wait, I think, for the e-court to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 22 in English, D1464 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it marked for identification, is it tendered --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, D1464 under seal is 65 ter 1D6189. The report that Mr. Ivetic is referring to is 1D6184 which has not been tendered as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I stand corrected, and if we can have 1D06184, and it will be page 22 in English, and page 29 in the Serbian, and paragraph 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, professor, in the approximate middle of that paragraph, you have a line that reads as follows: "As already said, such tables are of no demographic significance in the sense of representing specific demographic indicators." And this is in relation to Annex 3 of Dr. Tabeau's report entitled: Index of victims identification documents collected to date, source: BH Office of the Prosecutor. Could you please explain your comments.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the table shows when each of the documents was received by the OTP and whether it's under seal or not, in which language it is, and so on. In the demographic sense, that has no importance whatsoever, for the simple reason that if you state the sources of information, it's unimportant on what date you received which document. It's a rather large table, and I really do not understand its purpose, but it certainly has nothing to do with demographics. There's no demographic information that you can draw from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in both languages of your report, and if we could focus on paragraph 69 of the same, and I'll wait for the screen to reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar informs me that the machine is frozen, which surprises me on the first day where the sun shines in the Netherlands, but apparently there's a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now it would appear that we have resolved whatever the problem was. So looking at paragraph 69 of your report, and it reads: "A preference for the broader context is pronounced in this report as well. The broader context encompasses missing persons from Prijedor as a universe for Tomasica victims. The results of the comprehensiveness (universe) of missing persons from Prijedor are based, as are all the other findings, on the powerful methodology. This is also attested to by the fact that the different reports of the same expert give different definitions of the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina (ARK). Different municipalities are thus added to or subtracted from the region, including municipalities of unknown disappearances, depending on what the expert thinks she needs. It is thus claimed that the database contains disappearances from 23 ARK municipalities during the period of 1992, including a number of cases with missing data on time and/or place of disappearance or incomplete personal details. This database was formed by matching PKM and ICRC lists. The expert conceals the criteria used for the matching in order to find a total of unique cases. A table, which is nothing but statistical exhibitionism, is presented. Let us see what the table looks like and what information exactly it gives or conceals." Can you explain what you mean here in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The table shows, at least judging by its title, all the cases from the database of persons from ARK who went missing in 1992. So you can see the source, 1998, 2002, I suppose it's the Prijedor Book of Dead. And then ICRC. And then the number of units found in those sources. And then overlaps, 4.615. Overlaps of what? It is a fact that the database of the Prijedor book from 2002 certainly contains many names from 1998. It's also a fact, as Dr. Tabeau later says, that the ICRC and the Prijedor books do not match in almost one-half of overlaps. So what does it mean, a total of unique cases? That the doctor singled out 4.615 unique cases from the ICRC and from the Prijedor book? This is a table that is absolutely impossible to understand. Only the doctor knows how she got this number of 4.615. If you have so many overlaps, that implies that you found something in several sources. That number of people. But what do unique cases mean? There are more overlaps than unique cases. Each overlap should be a unique case. So I absolutely do not understand this table. And I think that its purpose here is to confuse. There is no explanation in the sense that she would say, Yes, here I used the same source of information from 1998 and 2002 have the same number of cases. Later on, she explains by saying that ICRC has 2000 and odd, and then I matched them so I have such and such a number. But it's all so confusing, I think she is the only one who know what she means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this paragraph where you talk about the changing definition of the ARK, what municipalities are included in the ARK, in footnote 75, you cite to the report for the Milomir Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that is 1D6191 in e-court in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that report, Dr. Tabeau has dealt with mortality statistics for Prijedor in these municipalities from 1991. Has Dr. Tabeau taken into account any mortality statistics for Prijedor or the ARK that existed in peacetime in relation to her Tomasica report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And not only for Tomasica. I've said a number of times Dr. Tabeau has not a single one statistical demographic indicator, and she knows exactly what those indicators are. It is also absurd, unless you note that in a footnote, that in a report you use something as a whole and in a different report something else, especially as these are different municipalities. So sometimes municipalities are taken into account or dropped and so on. And as for the broader context, Dr. Tabeau says that ARK contains 23 municipalities. I can understand that, but I don't understand why she needs it. What she's interested in here is Tomasica, and it's known exactly where this Tomasica is. So why show something that's not part of the task encompassed by the report? So if the tables say that the ARK contains 23 municipalities but then she reduces them to 15 and then she says, Well, we'll take only five municipalities that are contacted with the indictment and show that in the tables, without any explanation, I really don't understand what that is about. And if I don't understand it, because I think I understand demographics a little, then as there are no actual statistical indicators, then the broader context is very important. Especially as in her book she says that the broader context an imperative, though she doesn't say who set the imperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next I want to turn to your conclusions to be found on pages 24 to 25 of your report in English, and it will be pages 32 through 33 of your report in the Serbian, and that will be beginning with paragraph number 72 and going to paragraph number 73. First of all, do you stand by the conclusions as written in your report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I could pay particular attention to the second part of paragraph 72, which will be on the same page in the Serbian in the middle of the page, and it will be on the next page in the English, and it will be the second paragraph of item number 72, and it reads as follows: "Since appropriate scientific standards cannot be applied to inappropriate data sources, the only way out is the application of a 'powerful methodology' which is contrary to all the rules of the statistical and demographic profession and science. This methodology is not practiced anywhere in the world except for the 'court' analyses of the Prosecution expert. This methodology allows a selective choice of data sources, modification of standard statistical and demographic methods, and concealment of the criteria according to which these methods are applied, invention of new methods, inclusion in identified persons of recovered persons for whom final DNA findings still do not exist or whose DNA findings do not match the DNA findings of family members, correction of cause of death, insinuation that solely executed civilian victims are in question despite the existence of documents showing that there had been fighting also, presentation of statistical indicators which have nothing to do with demography (gun-shots statistics) and review of the 'broader context' which is on no grounds associated with Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa." Do you have any further explanations that you'd like to give to us in relation to this paragraph of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that this is a conclusion based on everything that I studied and reviewed. This is all that I could draw as a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at paragraph 73 of the report, which is on the next page in the Serbian, on the same page in English, and it reads: "The application of a powerful methodology produces targeted statistical results. Targeted statistical results are not a genuine contribution to finding scientifically grounded truth but their presentation may cause confusion and impose a distorted picture of the nature and extent of the events under analysis." I would stop right there and ask you: Can you explain for us what is the reliability of such targeted statistical results?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as they are targeted, it means that they cannot be reliable. And the overall methodology, which as we have seen is not in accordance with the academic one and the one usually applied but is, rather, powerful, is not recognised anywhere as a scientific methodology. It is constructed in order to obtain the targeted results; that is to say, to meet the criteria set by the Prosecution and implying high numbers. They do not explain what the criteria are, but they believe that such criteria need to be met. And she's trying to avoid the official sources based on which mortality is deduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, how are such targeted statistical findings treated in the field of scientific demography?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one uses them as relevant. The fact that they are targeted means they're not relevant. In scientific demography, it is simply not the usual practice. The problem here is that the Prosecution expert divides analyses into court analyses and other analyses. And I have quoted this exactly, what they mean already in Srebrenica here, perhaps it's in a footnote. Because Trial Chambers do not comprise experts in methodologies, so let's not burden them with methodology but, rather, write a court analysis. But there are no court and other methodologies. There is scientific methodology and those that are not scientific.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would tender the report of Professor Radovanovic, which is 65 ter number 1D06184, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually decide on admission, I think, when we have heard the whole of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless, at this moment, Mr. File, you'd like to express yourself on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I believe the customary way of addressing it should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Registrar, the number under which the report would be marked for identification would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1484, Your Honours, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Ms. Radovanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. File. You'll find Mr. File to your right. Mr. File is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. File, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: During your testimony last week starting at transcript page 43721, line 23, you said: "I cannot claim that certain sections in some reports are not acceptable, but I can assert with a great degree of certainty that some parts from a large number of the expert reports are absolutely unacceptable in the methodological sense." Now, we're here to talk about Dr. Tabeau's report on Tomasica victims. Could you share with us which sections of that report - and I'm using your double negative now - that you cannot claim are not acceptable?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning Tomasica, mainly all parts. But I could accept if Dr. Tabeau had used, for instance, the records of identification she received from the prosecution. These records -- I mean the prosecution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These records of identification are the basis for issuing death certificates. I stress that the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in my experience, because I also work as an expert in Sarajevo, also has not only the records but also the death certificates. I don't know whether the doctor requested them, but she received the records --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So, Dr. Radovanovic --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are 180 of them. I could accept them as an official source.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It sounds to me like you're issuing an another critique. And my question: Was which parts of the report do you agree with?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I disagree with all parts of the report regarding Tomasica. That's the first thing I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have P7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then first -- you were quoted to have said, I've not verified it yet: "I cannot claim that certain sections in some reports are acceptable, but I can assert," and then you said what you were disagreeing with. The question was: Which are the parts, which are the sections and of what reports of which you cannot claim that they are not acceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said some reports. Reports, in the plural. Specifically concerning Tomasica, there is no section in the Tomasica report that is acceptable from the point of view of scientific demography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But now what -- and then in other reports, if you say, well, in Tomasica report, nothing, but you said: Some reports there are portions which I cannot claim that they are wrong. What reports, what sections, do you -- had you -- did you have in mind when you said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a misunderstanding. I said I can't claim that some sections of some reports. What I mean is I've read several reports by Dr. Tabeau, not only the Tomasica report, and some sections in some reports I could accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's all understood. But you are invited to identify which parts of which reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Tomasica is concerned, not a single section. As far as some other reports are concerned, if you want me to specify now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I talk about other reports? What I could accept? All the reports by Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just say: This section of that report. Not to explain in full, but first to identify which sections of which reports you do not take issue with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I would have to run all the reports through my head. Could I answer this question after the break? Because I've read countless reports, in fact, many reports by Dr. Tabeau. What I can remember now is the report from 2013 that she wrote for the Stanisic and Simatovic case, I believe. She fairly cites all the sources for war casualties and these are all proper demographic sources, but she states these sources relatively correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please look at P7453, page 9 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: As this comes up, you'll see this is the PowerPoint presentation that you were just looking at earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The frost is striking again. Mr. File, there seems to be a technical error. Is there any way, since I think everything that is in the PowerPoint presentation is taken from the report, that you could refer to the relevant page of the report, hoping that that can be produced on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I can do that. Although I believe there was a percentage at issue that may not be reproduced in the report, so I will move to a different area and then come back to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to your own report, which has been marked for identification as D1484. We may not be able to put this on the screen for you, but I believe you have a hard copy in front of you that you can refer to. I'd like to refer to you - and everyone - to English page 7, B/C/S page 8. And this will be paragraph 14 at the bottom. So at the end of this paragraph, you say: "The question is why in drawing up her reports for the Prosecution the expert witness does not respect recognised and known international standards in preparing statistical and demographic analyses." It's true that in this report you do not cite any textbooks on statistics or demography that describe the recognised and known international standards have you in mind; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not citing them. But in paragraph 13, I cite what Dr. Tabeau says without a reference. I can answer as to what is considered recognised and known.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If you could just focus on the questions that I ask you. My next question is that you also do not cite any scientific or scholarly journals that describe these recognised and known international standards in statistics or demography; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I quote Dr. Tabeau, and she knows well what is internationally known and recognised, as you see from paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And where do you quote Dr. Tabeau referring to a recognised and known international standard that you refer to in your report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Footnote 2. Dr. Tabeau says this without quoting, this is internationally known and recognised. Because when you are in that science, you know that very well. In the 2005 report of Dr. Tabeau, I again quote Dr. Tabeau's sources for mortality, what are good and what are bad statistical sources, and through my report, you can see that I refer to it. I cite it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we look at --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was understood that we, between experts, know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You referred to paragraph 13 and footnote 2 of your report. In paragraph 13, you say: "In a publication intended for the broad public, the Prosecution expert witness observes in reference to the reports of demographers engaged by the Office of the Prosecutor that 'whenever a demographic expert report is admitted'" --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot follow you. You are reading from paragraph 13; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll continue: "'... the likely consequence is that the report has impact on the judgement,' in contrast to reports from the opposite side, although 'a vast majority of the work of Defence experts unfortunately cannot be seen as up to international scientific standards.'" So this reference that you made also does not describe the known and recognised international standards that you refer to; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a quotation. I cannot describe it. I am quoting Dr. Tabeau who is an expert in demography and who is competent to judge what are and aren't internationally recognised standards. And if Dr. Tabeau did not quote it from a textbook, I thought it was absurd for me to quote it. But, again, I repeat, I can explain it if it's not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, just to be clear, the only source that you refer to, according to you, in your report as justification for what the international standards in statistics and demography are, is the Prosecution expert; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you allow me, I have a Ph.D. in demography and I surely know what are international standards and what are not. I suppose that since Dr. Tabeau is the same, she knows it as well, and she needs not explain to another expert in her field. I didn't think I should cite textbooks because I am an expert, and I'm the most qualified in demography in this courtroom. If somebody finds something incorrect, inaccurate in my report, please go ahead. I do not think I need to cite textbooks, but I'm ready and willing to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- I -- Judge Moloto may have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, your report is intended to give an opinion to this Court. It's not intended as a letter to or a -- a document that is sent to Dr. Tabeau. So we are not demographers, so if you say Dr. Tabeau is wrong in -- from the point of view of the principles of demography, you've got to say to us what -- on what basis you say she is wrong judged against internationally accepted demographic principles. So we understand that you have got a Ph.D. in demography and therefore you may not need to quote your authorities if you are talking to Dr. Tabeau. But you are not talking to Dr. Tabeau. You are talking to this Court. And this Court is lay in demography, and it expects to be guided by your professional opinion which should be based on internationally accepted principles which we don't know and so you've got to give them to us. Okay? And that's the thrust of the question from Mr. File. You don't tell us by what standards you're judging Dr. Tabeau. You just say internationally accepted, but you're not giving us the specific standard that judges that part of the -- of demography, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe through this examination I have said that, and I've also put it in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's what Mr. File is asking you, that where in your report do you give the internationally accepted demographic standard against which you critique Mrs. Tabeau. He is asking you to guide him into your report where you give such standards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my conclusion at the end, when I say she uses this, that, and that, it means all of that is contrary to international standards. I have tried, through the examination and the report, to say that in international standards there is no methodology that is called powerful. There is a methodology called scientific and it's based on relevant sources of data for mortality, and it is known exactly - and I'm quoting Dr. Tabeau - that is, the death certificate, based on the register of deaths and the court decisions. It's based on the statistical method of matching called match, or overlap, but only if used properly, and I've explained here what properly means; whereas Dr. Tabeau provides 72 criteria. That is not an international standard. Furthermore, I have shown that the sources used by Dr. Tabeau have absolutely no relation to demographic sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I stop you there, please. Unfortunately, you're not -- we've heard all this evidence that you've given us, but you're not addressing the question that is being put to you. What Mr. File is asking you is: You are not quoting authorities in demography in your report against which you judge Madam Tabeau. Would you answer that question: Yes, you do or you don't; no, I do. And if I do, you can point to us on your footnotes where those authorities are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I understood you. If you mean that I put in a footnote saying scientifically recognised standards are these sources, this method, et cetera, no, I haven't done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we try turning back to P7453, and we'll hope it works this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask you a question that I think is probably far beneath your Ph.D. level, it's just an arithmetic question. It's based on your testimony at transcript page 20 from today, line 19. When you were talking about these two tables you said: "The error here lies in the fact that Dr. Tabeau counts the unavailable as Muslims, and she says there is -- are 95 per cent of Muslims, which is not correct. If there are 330, if I see well, it's not 95 per cent of the total. It's about 80-something per cent. And you can see that very well in this next part where she talks about Prijedor and the ARK. Look at the unavailable, 522. The field is blank. And these 522 is about 20 per cent of the total. And, again, Dr. Tabeau ascribes it all to Muslims. How does she know that these unavailable are Muslim by ethnicity? Muslims are 80-plus per cent, if these 522 are about 20 per cent of the total." Now, if you look at the table on the left, if you take the Muslim number, which is 320, and you add Croat number, which is 1, the other number, which is 12, and Serb number, which is 1, you get a total of 334. And if you take the Muslim number of 320, and you divide it by 334, you get 95.8 per cent, which is the per cent that Dr. Tabeau presents here. So the fact is, she's not counting unavailable as Muslims. She's just giving the per cent of the available; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dr. Tabeau says here: Total, 378, not 334. And Dr. Tabeau maintains that 378 is the number of victims in Tomasica. What Dr. Tabeau means and whether her arithmetics are correct, I don't know, but the fact is that out of 378, Muslims do not account for 95.8 per cent. If she made a correction, then she should have taken into account the total. If the total is 378, then 320 is not 95 per cent. And if the total is not 378, then why write it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would also -- I would also point to the table on the right. If you add all of those first four numbers together for the available information, you get a total of 2058, and if you divide 1953 by 2058, you get 94.9 per cent again. Now, I understand you're relying on what the number says at the bottom row, but this is very easy to figure out if you see what this breakdown is; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, it's not 2058. It's 2580. And the table should not be designed for us to make an effort to understand what Dr. Tabeau meant. But somebody asked the question - I mean Judge Moloto - whether these 13 per cent should be deleted. Dr. Tabeau says yes. In the second table, where the total is 2580, 1600-something, the percentage is not right. It's 74 per cent or something, not what is written here. Apart from that, how can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll cut this matter short. It's clear that the totals include the unavailable. It seems also clear that in the percentages, the unavailable were excluded, which is not a very transparent way of presenting these tables. It also explains why the 13.2 per cent should be taken out if you want to present the ethnicity of those for whom the ethnicity is an available datum. If you want to present something else, that is, that you want to present what the percentage of Muslims is on the total, that is, available ethnicity, not available ethnicity, then, of course, the percentages are different. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what Dr. Tabeau means. I see what she writes. I really don't know. I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking if you agree with what I said, which includes some criticism on Dr. Tabeau because she is not consistent, but I tried to explain what you could understand from this and I wonder whether you agreed with me. And if you want to re-read it, then -- well, no, you can't -- well, in English you can re-read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't agree with you for the simple reason that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. No, that's good. Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I think we're at the time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at the time for a break. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers that it's sufficiently informed about the matter you raised, about the calculations, percentages, et cetera, in relation to this table in relation to the questions that were put to the witness. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Ms. Radovanovic. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we wait for the witness, I did want to perhaps raise a matter. During the last session, at temporary transcript page 23, lines 16 through 18, my colleague on the other side, Mr. File, talked about what he called a matching log which is different from the matching keys or criteria we've been discussing. I want it place on the record that the Prosecution has never disclosed to the Defence any matching log as a -- bearing that title. We believe that this is therefore, if it exists, in violation of the rules as to expert testimony. Because from the Martic decision on Prosecution motion for admission of transcripts pursuant to Rule 92 bis and of expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of 13 January 2006 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down if you want to have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, before we start talking about the hypothetical, Mr. File, I understood your observation to be that Mr. Ivetic is now asking for something different, that is, a log, and you -- at least I didn't have the impression but please correct me when I'm wrong, I didn't have the impression that you thought that it would exist or -- but that it's just that you drew our attention to the fact that Mr. Ivetic was asking for something he had not asked for before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's precisely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, on the hypothetical, then please sit together with Mr. File, ask him whether he considers what he says you asked for in addition to what you asked before, whether he thinks that exists. If it exists, then the issue of disclosure, I think, becomes relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I move to my second point. On the cross-examination list for this witness, we have 65 ter number 33824 which has just been disclosed to us, which says it's a table when you open up the document. It's under seal so I won't reference the name of the individual involved. But it says: Criteria for checking. So, in essence, this is criteria, not a log. We've never had this before. We checked the ERN range and that was not disclosed on the EDS system. And it pertains to one named victim. So if these exist as to other named victims, I do believe that the Prosecution has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- acted outside of the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to focus on the facts. Is there one or is there such a document for all victims, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that Mr. Ivetic is referring to doesn't have anything to do with this issue that we're discussing right now, and it may be used in cross-examination but it's not -- it's not about this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- I think Mr. Ivetic was raising a disclosure issue, rather. If there's any reason to pursue that, Mr. Ivetic, after you've heard the questions in cross-examination, you can deal with the matter in re-examination. And if it is relevant and if there's a disclosure issue, we'll certainly pay proper attention to once it is raised at that point in time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could please have D1484 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is your report again. We're going to look at English page 10, B/C/S page 13, which is paragraph 24 of your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So here you're pointing out that Ewa Tabeau's Tomasica report does not repeat a point that she made in an academic journal article that she co-authored. The quotation that you cite says: "Only a few sources can be taken as safe and sound, for instance, records from death certificates, court decisions proclaiming persons dead, and death records of armed forces from the archives of the Ministry of Defence." You also testified about this point, starting at T.43697. Now we're going to look at this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's 1D06187, please. I think the transcript says 16. It's 1D06187.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So here you see Dr. Tabeau's article in the European Journal of Population from 2005. The title is: "War-related deaths in the 1992-1995 armed conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina: A critique of previous estimates and recent results." And if you go a little further down in the page, you see where it says "abstract," it says: "In this article, we provide a critique of previous estimates of war-related deaths from Bosnia and Herzegovina and propose an analytical framework and a new estimate of such deaths." So, from this, you would agree that the context of Dr. Tabeau's article here relates to the issue of an estimate of all war-related deaths in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to English page 12, B/C/S page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Just directing your attention to the headings on this page, at the bottom of the B/C/S, the heading says this is section 3.1, which relates to the sources and methods Dr. Tabeau's team used to generate an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now if we could go to English page 15 and B/C/S page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So looking at the paragraph in the middle of the page in both versions, you see Dr. Tabeau discussing the challenges in obtaining reliable data about war deaths. This paragraph starts by saying: "The next difficulty with data on war-related deaths is that persons reported in certain sources as dead or missing sometimes could have survived without their families notifying the appropriate authorities." And then we have the sentence that you extracted for your report about a few sources that can be taken as safe and sound. So this paragraph is about the potential problem that a given source could erroneously describe someone as dead who is actually alive, causing statistical estimates to lose accuracy; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this kind of source is not used in scientific research which Dr. Tabeau says in the previous paragraph only such and such sources, yes, and the fact that she has the following difficulties with data, that's a fact because she uses sources that are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So is that a yes as to what this paragraph is about?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. Can you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I was just asking you how you understand or read this paragraph. It's about the potential problem that a given source could erroneously describe someone as dead who is actually alive, causing statistical estimates to lose accuracy. That's what this paragraph is about; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This paragraph explains in principle all possible problems of sources that are relevant for demography and warns the professional public of what is normally used. We use other sources and we have the following problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So I'm a little confused as to how you receive the meaning of this relating to, as you said, "all possible problems of sources that are relevant for demography," when the first sentence of this paragraph says that it relates to data on war-related deaths, and then it goes on to say "that persons reported in certain sources as dead or missing" - certain sources as dead or missing - "sometimes could have survived without their families notifying the appropriate authorities." Where do you get "all possible problems of sources that are relevant for demography" from that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the ICRC source. It has to do with the ICRC source, the Prijedor books of the dead, those are sources where, for example, someone's reported as dead and then it turns out that he is alive. And in the Tomasica report, Dr. Tabeau says - I don't remember whether it's for 2005 or some other year - that it's been established and so and so are alive, by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. The Tomasica report relates to the process of counting and identifying dead people who have been exhumed from mass graves in Tomasica and in some cases linked to Jakarina Kosa; correct? That's what that report is about?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. Also the missing persons. There's a series of tables that have to do primarily with the ARK and that where she talks about the missing persons. I can't tell you off the top of my head, but I can look whether she talks about the dead from Tomasica in a table or whether she talks about the missing persons. The places where they went missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's fine. So related to the part of the report that relates to the process of counting and identifying dead people who have been exhumed from mass graves, the question of whether a source is a reliable indicator that someone is dead is not at issue for this part of the report; right? We already know these people are dead.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
